stories.headline: Russia strikes Kyiv as Moscow signals readiness to resume US-mediated Ukraine peace talks

sources.body:
Experts say Russia is trying to destroy energy infrastructure before winter and US ‘appeasement and flattery’ will not achieve peace

Russia has carried out a massive “demonstrative” attack on Ukraine, bombarding Kyiv with ballistic missiles just hours after Vladimir Putin said he had agreed to resume trilateral negotiations after talks with the US envoy Steve Witkoff.

Overnight, Moscow pounded the Ukrainian capital, killing at least two people and wounding 22, including four children. Targets included the southern bridge over the Dnipro River, civilian houses, energy infrastructure, an ambulance station, office buildings and a monastery.

The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy , said on Thursday that numerous sites across the city had been hit and damaged. Twelve regions across the country were bombed including the southern city of Odesa, where the port was badly hit.

Zelenskyy said the latest devastating strikes showed that Russia was not serious about peace. “Almost immediately after another round of talks, Russia launched a pointed attack. This means there has been no real change in its attitude toward everything that is happening,” he said.

During negotiations on Wednesday in St Petersburg, Witkoff lavished praise on Vladimir Putin , who was sitting across the table. “You talk so much about my president, President Trump, being a humanitarian. You are a humanitarian also, sir, and I salute that,” Witkoff said.

In a social media post after the strikes in the early hours of Thursday, Zelenskyy issued a sardonic reply. “Three waves of ballistic missiles have been launched at Kyiv by Russian ‘humanitarians’ since yesterday evening. They used 21 missiles,” he wrote.

Zelenskyy said he was grateful to those among Ukraine’s western partners who saw “the situation for what it is” and “acknowledged the reality” that the Kremlin had little intention of stopping its war. He called for stronger air defences, Patriot interceptors which could bring down enemy missiles and more sanctions against Moscow.

Ukraine’s foreign minister, ⁠Andrii Sybiha, ⁠added that “appeasement, ⁠servility ​and flattery” ‌would ‌not ‌stop Russian aggression.

On Wednesday, the Kremlin foreign affairs adviser Yuri Ushakov said Putin had agreed “in principle” to resume three-way negotiations involving Russia, the US and Ukraine after 10 November, a week after the US midterm elections. In reality, Russia’s real intention is to destroy Ukraine’s energy infrastructure, leaving millions in the dark and cold , officials in Kyiv believe.

According to Zelenskyy, the US has resumed intelligence warnings of Russian missile attacks. But the White House has so far not reversed the slowdown of Starshield, the military version of Elon Musk’s Starlink internet satellite system, leaving Ukraine unable to intercept enemy drones or carry out mid-range battlefield strikes.

The New York Times reported that when the slowdown was imposed last week, dozens of armed drones heading to Russian military targets fell from the sky. The video feeds streaming their flight paths suddenly went fuzzy as the connection with Starshield was lost, the paper said.
sources.headline: Russia bombards Kyiv with missiles hours after agreeing to resume talks with Ukraine

sources.body: Russia and Ukraine traded major drone and missile strikes on each other's capitals overnight, hours after Moscow signalled readiness to resume US-mediated peace talks. President Donald Trump said negotiations were closer than ever to ending the war, though the Kremlin expressed doubts over Ukrainian and European proposals.
sources.headline: Russia and Ukraine trade strikes overnight as Moscow signals readiness for peace talks

sources.body: A US envoy met Putin in Saint Petersburg on Wednesday after the Kremlin agreed to resume peace talks with Ukraine and the United States. Details by FRANCE 24's correspondent Gulliver Cragg.
sources.headline: Russia agrees to resume trilateral peace talks on Ukraine war

stories.headline: Houthi attacks kill civilians at a Saudi airport as the conflict threatens oil supplies and prompts US diplomatic departures

sources.body:
Yemen's Houthi movement has said it carried out an attack on an airport in eastern Saudi Arabia on Wednesday evening, which Saudi authorities said killed two people and injured eight others.

The Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation identified those killed at King Fahd International Airport in Dammam as a Saudi citizen and an Indian resident.

It did not say what type of attack occurred, but the Iran-backed Houthis said on Thursday that the airport was one of the sites they had targeted with drones and missiles over the previous 48 hours.

Two more people were killed on Wednesday morning by debris from a drone that was intercepted elsewhere in Eastern Province, the Saudi energy ministry said.

The drone was intercepted as it attempted to target a processing facility owned by Saudi Arabia's state oil company Aramco in the Shaybah oil field, where a contractor's vehicle was set ablaze, according to the ministry.

It identified the dead as residents from the Philippines and Nepal.

The Houthis' military spokesman, Yahya Sarea, did not claim the attack on the oil field.

In addition to Dammam's airport, he said they had targeted the Saudi defence ministry's headquarters building in the capital, Riyadh, an Aramco facility in the Red Sea city of Yanbu, and Abha International Airport in the south of the country.

The Saudi-led coalition supporting the Yemeni government in its war against the Houthis said four drones were intercepted over Eastern Province on Wednesday night, and that another four were intercepted over the provinces of Riyadh and Medina on Thursday.

At least 21 people have now been killed in Houthi attacks on Saudi airports since the start of October, according to Saudi authorities.

One missile strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October killed 13 people and injured 308 others – the deadliest attack in Saudi Arabia in more than a decade.

The Houthis also reiterated on Thursday that they had attacked Saudi Arabia in retaliation for deadly Saudi air strikes on the territory they control in western Yemen.

Houthi-run media reported on Wednesday night that at least six people had been killed and 11 injured in air and artillery strikes over the previous 24 hours.

According to the Houthi-run health ministry, 155 civilians have been killed since Yemen's devastating civil war flared up three months ago.

The government's health ministry has said at least 1,574 people have been killed in the conflict over the same period.

The fighting has also displaced more than 256,000 people.

The war began in 2014, when the Houthis ousted the internationally-recognised government from the capital, Sanaa. The conflict escalated the next year, after the Saudi-led coalition of Arab states intervened in an attempt to restore the government's rule.

A four-year-old informal ceasefire began to unravel in July, when the Houthis announced a "maritime embargo" against Saudi Arabia and began missile and drone attacks on Saudi airports, oil facilities, and tankers in the Red Sea.

The Houthis said they were retaliating for what they call a Saudi blockade of their territory, as well as an air strike on Sanaa airport that they blamed on the kingdom.
sources.headline: Two killed in Houthi attack on airport in eastern Saudi Arabia, authorities say

sources.body:
Similar withdrawals from UAE, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain reported as concerns grow about restart of war on Iran after US midterm elections

The US state department has ordered some diplomats and the families of US government employees to leave Saudi Arabia as the gulf kingdom faces a barrage of near-daily attacks, with at least three people killed at an airport and oilfield.

Attacks on “civilian airports and other critical infrastructure” by the Iranian-supported Houthis in Yemen were highlighted as the reason for the drawdown. The state department spokesperson, Tommy Pigott, said: “The safety and security of department personnel and their families remain our highest priority.”

The state department said the order covered its embassy in Riyadh and its satellite consulates. The embassy had been badly damaged at the start of the US war on Iran and had been operating with only a skeleton staff for months, although in recent weeks some diplomats had returned.

Media outlets – including NBC and AFP – reported that families of US embassy personnel were also being withdrawn from the United Arab Emirates, Jordan, Qatar and Bahrain, while the New York Times said the Trump administration was developing plans to restart the war on Iran.

However, in his statement on Wednesday, Pigott described the reports of further withdrawals as “inaccurate” and said the state department order was for the departure of staff and their families from Saudi Arabia only.

Saudi Arabia has faced a succession of deadly attacks from the Houthis over recent weeks, including a strike on Riyadh’s international airport which was the kingdom’s deadliest in years as the war with the group escalates.

On Thursday the Saudi Civil Aviation Authority announced that two people had been killed in overnight attacks on King Fahd international airport in Dammam on the Gulf near Bahrain and Qatar.

Eight people were injured and there was material damage to the airport, according to officials. The global flight-tracking service Flightradar24 said flights had been diverted away from the airport.

Separately, falling debris from the successful interception of a drone targeting an oil facility in the country’s south-east killed two people and injured a further two, the Saudi energy ministry said.

The Houthis said on Thursday ⁠they ⁠had ​launched attacks on ⁠Saudi Arabia’s defence ministry in ⁠Riyadh, Saudi ​Aramco ‌facilities ‌in Yanbu ‌and King Fahd international airport in Dammam.

Essential workers at Saudi Aramco’s headquarters in the east of the country were told to evacuate on Thursday, two sources told Agence France-Presse, after their non-essential colleagues were told to work from home since last week.

The US previously ordered non-essential staff to leave the Gulf in late February before the start of its war against Iran. NBC reported that the US military had been quietly scaling back its presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, but a spokesperson from US central command told the US news outlet that service members were regularly moved to “optimize mission readiness”.
sources.headline: Some US diplomats told to leave Saudi Arabia amid Houthi attacks

Iran’s IRGC says it hit four vessels in the northern Gulf and three more struck mines near the strait of Hormuz

Shipping workers: how is the Middle East conflict affecting you?

Oil prices jumped to a five-month high on Thursday after ​attacks in Saudi Arabia and hits to tankers in the strait of Hormuz threatened further disruptions to the world’s crude supply.

Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by 3% to hit $112 a barrel for first time since 18 May.

Yemeni Houthis , who are aligned with Iran, hit several targets in Saudi Arabia on Wednesday, with two people killed and eight more wounded in a civilian airport in Dammam, and two people killed in a drone attack on a Saudi oilfield.

Elsewhere the Iranian Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said four vessels involved in “illegal” oil transfers in the northern ​Gulf were hit and caught fire after being tracked by its forces on Wednesday.

It said three more vessels collided with mines west of the strait of Hormuz, and warned the US that continued provocations could lead to a wider response against its regional bases.

The US has now ordered some diplomats and family members to leave their missions in Saudi Arabia, and it plans to withdraw family members from a number of other missions in the Middle East, according to Reuters, which also reported that Saudi Aramco has instructed staff to evacuate its headquarters in Dhahran and work remotely.

Concern is growing that conflict in the region could escalate further, almost eight months after Tehran’s effective block on the strait of Hormuz triggered what many feared would bring the greatest energy supply disruption in the history of the market. In the first weeks after the US-Israeli attacks on Iran , oil surged past $100 a barrel and market observers predicted prices of up to $150 a barrel as flows through Hormuz came to a halt.

Oil peaked at $126 a barrel in April during the conflict and fell back below $100 in late May and then to lows of $71 at the start of July amid hopes of a ceasefire in the region. The price began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and fresh hostilities broke out in the Gulf .

However, data from Kpler has shown that oil exports from the Persian Gulf have now risen above their prewar levels, partly because of an increase in oil pumped overland through pipelines to the Red Sea and Gulf of Oman.

Global stocks wobbled on Thursday amid expectations of higher inflation and borrowing costs. The Stoxx Europe 600, which tracks the biggest companies on the continent, fell by 1%, with the UK’s FTSE 100 down by 0.7%.

Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning

In Asia, Japan’s Nikkei 225 index dropped 2.7%, while the South Korean Kospi fell 3.5%. Hong Kong’s Hang Seng index shed 3%.

Shares in American Airlines dropped almost 4% in pre-market trading after the company warned that high fuel costs would push it into a loss this year.
sources.headline: Oil prices jump to five-month high as attacks threaten global supply

stories.headline: Iran unveils an offensive military doctrine as Trump hints at possible action before the November vote

sources.body:
US orders diplomatic staff out of Saudi Arabia amid escalating conflict and reports of potential US and Israeli strikes on Iran.

Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) says renewed attacks by the United States could prompt Tehran to invade neighbouring countries and hit bases used in US military operations as part of its new “offensive” strategy.

The warning on Wednesday came amid escalating attacks on shipping in the Strait of Hormuz, a global energy chokepoint, and uncertainty over diplomatic efforts to end the nearly eight-month war.

“Our defence doctrine was previously defensive; we used to say that if a country attacks us, we will respond. Now we say that if a country attacks us, we will both respond and launch an offensive,” IRGC spokesman Hossein Mohebi said.

Washington ordered some diplomatic personnel to leave Saudi Arabia amid attacks from Yemen’s Houthis while US President Donald Trump has signalled that a decision on the conflict could come soon.

According to media reports, the US and Israel are planning potential attacks on Iran in the coming weeks.

As negotiations seem stalled and both sides exchange threats, could the region be heading towards another military escalation?

The IRGC on Wednesday announced a shift towards an “offensive and asymmetrical” defence doctrine, threatening to invade countries that launch attacks against it.

Mohebi said Tehran would no longer limit its military operations to retaliatory strikes.

Mohebi stressed that Iran’s missile stockpile has increased 1.5 times since the 12-day war between Iran and Israel in June 2025. He did not provide specific figures.

“The quality of the missiles has improved significantly, and their range, destructive power and accuracy in hitting targets have increased,” the spokesman said.

Moreover, Mohebi said Iranian forces were in the “stage of preparing to unveil the ‘father of all bombs’. This is something new for the enemy.”

Meanwhile, attacks in the Strait of Hormuz continued unabated.

The IRGC’s navy said on Thursday that four vessels it accused of being involved in illegal oil transfers were struck and caught fire in the northern Gulf. Three other vessels hit mines west of the strait, it added.

Before the war, one-fifth of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies passed through the Strait of Hormuz. While shipments through the strait are still below those levels, oil shipments from the region returned to pre-war levels last month as exporters found alternative ways to ship out their oil and gas, including using pipelines.

However, a flurry of recent attacks in the key waterway and the fighting between Yemen’s Houthis and its Saudi-backed, internationally recognised government, which has resulted in Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia, have once again sent oil prices surging. Brent crude climbed above $110 a barrel on Thursday amid fears of further disruptions to regional energy supplies.

Iran’s shift towards an offensive military doctrine reflects Tehran’s determination to make future US-Israeli attacks significantly more costly, according to analysts.
sources.headline: Iran reveals ‘offensive’ doctrine, US issues alert: Is war imminent?

El presidente Donald Trump después de aterrizar en la base de Andrews, en Maryland

La guerra en Irán no ha terminado. La campaña para las elecciones legislativas en Israel y Estados Unidos, el 27 de octubre y el 3 de noviembre, ha supuesto una pausa en las hostilidades, pero tanto Tel Aviv como Washington ya elaboran planes específicos para reanudar los bombardeos, según  The New York Times  y otros medios estadounidenses citando a altos cargos de la Casa Blanca.

Ambos países han intensificado en los últimos días las maniobras militares en la región, incluidos sobrevuelos a Irak para practicar operaciones de bombardeo, y prevén ejecutar nuevos ataques pasados los comicios de EE.UU., en los que el elevado precio de la energía, consecuencia de la guerra, se ha convertido en un asunto impopular que está pasando factura a los republicanos.

El secretario de Defensa, Pete Hegseth, se reunió esta semana en secreto con el primer ministro israelí, Beniamin Netanyahu, en la base aérea de Ovda, en el sur de Israel, donde abordaron la planificación de estos nuevos ataques. Según el periódico estadounidense, los objetivos incluirían infraestructuras energéticas de Irán, sus instalaciones nucleares y su arsenal de misiles y drones. Con una nueva gran oleada de ataques, el Pentágono calcula que llevará a la debilitada economía iraní al borde del colapso y Teherán se verá obligado a hacer concesiones.

La intención es dar una estocada final al régimen de los ayatolás, liderado por Mojtaba Jamenei tras la muerte de su padre Alí el 28 de febrero, el día en el que comenzó la operación conjunta de EE.UU. e Israel. Mientras Donald Trump, inmerso en una gira de campaña por todo el país, minimiza las consecuencias de la guerra y la da por ganada, Netanyahu está hablando con mayor claridad sobre sus objetivos.

El miércoles, insistió durante una ceremonia de graduación de oficiales de las Fuerzas de Defensa de Israel (FDI) en que Jamenei “ha decidido seguir los pasos de su padre” y está intentando “desarrollar una vez más las bombas de la muerte”, en alusión a la bomba nuclear.

El presidente de EE.UU. ha dicho públicamente que no ordenará más ataques antes de las elecciones legislativas de mitad de mandato, pero siempre ha dejado abierta la posibilidad de bombardear Irán después. Sin embargo, nada asegura que una nueva oleada de bombardeos permita poner fin a la guerra o tenga mayor éxito que la primera fase de la guerra, en la que Washington agotó gran parte de su arsenal de misiles balísticos e interceptores al repeler los ataques de represalia iraníes.

Por su parte, Irán ha prometido su respuesta más contundente hasta la fecha si el enemigo reanuda su ofensiva. Concretamente, sus líderes han afirmado que ampliarán sus objetivos más allá de los buques comerciales en Ormuz, estrecho bloqueado desde el inicio de la guerra, y las infraestructuras energéticas y bases militares de los aliados de EE.UU. en la región: también pretenden incluir los centros de datos y los cables submarinos de internet.
sources.headline: EE.UU. e Israel se preparan para reanudar sus bombardeos sobre Irán

stories.headline: Governments rush to patch major PHP vulnerabilities affecting millions of websites

sources.body:
I once worked opposite a site where a shopping centre was being built.

We were warned there might be unexploded bombs from World War Two unearthed during the construction.

In the end, there were none, but procedures were put in place as a precaution and we all had to practice filing into designated safe zones inside our building.

The PHP story feels like the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb - I have never seen such a dramatic, public and global response to a cyber event that hasn't happened yet.

There has been no painful attack like the ransomware we saw knock out M&S and JLR in 2025.

But the potential threat is so serious that websites around the world have been taken down as a precaution.

Less than two months ago , 100 tech companies wrote an open letter warning the world to adopt a new level of cyber resilience in the age of AI.

It turns out we didn't have to wait very long to find out what they meant.

The weaknesses found in the PHP programming language, which is used by millions of websites, had been quietly resting there for years and are not easy to exploit.

One cyber security researcher told me he'd been up all night trying to do it as an experiment, but it was proving very difficult.

However, things that are very difficult for humans are increasingly very little trouble for AI.

The tech is getting a lot of credit here for assisting researchers in finding the bugs, and the PHP foundation, which oversees the programming language, was on the case and issued a fix.

It was supposed to be kept quiet until everyone had a chance to fix their sites - but the news was leaked.

From that point the clock started ticking.

As I write this, there are no reports that anyone or anything has succeeded in using the flaws to attack a site.

"There's a real dilemma," said Prof Alan Woodward from Surrey University.

"How do you alert people they need to be ready, and then that a patch is urgently required, whilst not alerting attackers?

"Basically you're telling everyone about the problem at the same time and hoping the defenders aren't awake enough to act as soon as the patch is out."

But we do know from large web companies like Cloudflare and Palo Alto Networks that millions of attempts have been made.

We probably won't know for a while whether it has worked for any criminals, because the companies affected might not be aware yet either.

As far as we know the unexploded bomb remains intact for now, and for some experts this is a success.

Gina Neff, Professor of Responsible AI at Queen Mary University, described this as a good news story.

"We've seen how a team of people supported by the large AI company have used AI to find the problem, work for months together to solve it and get everybody ready to be safe and secure," she told the Today Programme on BBC Radio 4.

"We have enormous capability to handle these risks."

But the baddies can use AI too, and those same tools are probably churning away right now trying to get in.

Cyber security authorities are warning website owners to fix the weaknesses immediately, but the patch only works on the latest version of PHP, so older sites will need to upgrade first.
sources.headline: Zoe Kleinman: PHP is the cyber equivalent of an unexploded bomb

sources.body: As governments and corporations alike scramble to install a patch to fix fundamental security flaws in a programming language that helps run roughly 70 percent of the world's websites, here's what you need to know about how AI has helped bring these critical vulnerabilities to light.
sources.headline: 'Backbone of the web': What is PHP and how has it raised AI hacking fears?

stories.headline: France moves to ban unsanctioned protests after violent unrest, allowing only union-organized demonstrations

sources.body:
Only authorised union protests will be allowed in French towns and cities on Saturday, President Emmanuel Macron has said, after demonstrations across the country turned violent last weekend.

Speaking as some cities including Lyon and Nice imposed complete bans, Macron said "illegitimate" protests would not be allowed but unions would be offered alternative routes so that businesses could be protected.

Big demonstrations against the high cost of living and school conditions were overshadowed last Saturday by riots and looting that saw business and historic buildings destroyed.

Interior Minister Jean-Didier Berger said police deployments would be increased by 20% compared to last weekend, after the government was accused of being blindsided by the scale of the unrest.

France's justice minister said on Thursday that 217 people had been jailed over last weekend's disorder after being convicted in fast-track trials, with that number expected to rise.

Gérald Darmanin said 2,700 people had been arrested across France and more than 1,000 have appeared in court.

Half of those detained had no prior criminal record, he said, according to Le Figaro newspaper.

Macron met intelligence services and ministers on Thursday, to prepare for the next national day of protests on Saturday.

"The general recommendation is that there should be no demonstrations. Those who want to continue to demonstrate, when they are trade union organisations, will have alternative routes proposed by the prefects," the French president announced. "When they're not union organisations, wherever possible, they'll be banned."

He attacked what he called "political and even seditious acts organised by far-left groups that aim to bring down the Republic".

Curfews were imposed in several cities in the aftermath of the weekend rioting, and Macron said the government wanted a return to calm.

The gilets jaunes (yellow-vest) movement was behind many of last weekend's protests and Paris authorities have said several of their proposed marches have been banned.

In Lyon, France's third-biggest city, regional authorities have imposed a blanket ban on demonstrations.

"In light of the mobilisation that is circulating and in view of the events of 17 October, the prefect has decided to prohibit by decree any demonstration in the city of Lyon this Saturday," the Rhône prefecture said in a statement.

Similar announcements have been made in Toulon on the south coast, the centre of Rouen in the north-west, and Grenoble in the east.

Partial curfews variously restricting the movement of young people and gatherings have been in place this week in cities including Marseille, Bordeaux, Nice and Lyon in the south as well as Lille and other towns in the north.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu promised a "massive" deployment of police officers this week to deal with any unrest this weekend, but some officers have told French media they are not trained to deal with large crowds.

Around 550,000 people took part in demonstrations on 17 October to protest rising fuel prices and the cost of living, which have escalated after weeks of student protests .
sources.headline: French weekend protests to be limited to union demos only, says Macron

sources.body:
Politicians have called for ruthless sentencing, but lawyers blame the politicians for the poverty, and anger, behind their clients’ looting

Awa, 18, stood in the dock in the tribunal de Paris , a small, mute and bewildered figure seeming unable to understand, let alone answer, the simplest of questions.

The court was told she had joined young people who looted an Yves Saint Laurent store on Boulevard Saint Germain in Paris’s Left Bank late on Sunday and stripped it bare within minutes.

Awa was arrested at a nearby Métro station with a black balaclava and black gloves in her backpack along with four YSL handbags worth a total of €5,000 (£4,200).

In the dock, dressed entirely in black – the clothes she was wearing when arrested two days earlier – she appeared panicked, clutched at her hair, picked her lip. Unable to speak, she covered her face and began to weep; first silently, then uncontrollably, her sobs punctuating an almost palpably painful silence.

Awa was just one of 2,500 people arrested during last weekend’s rioting and looting across the country , more than 900 of whom are being fast-tracked through the courts using a procedure called comparution immédiate (immediate appearance). It sends them to trial straight or shortly after being taken into custody, or within three days if they are held in pretrial detention.

The process of handling this sudden influx of cases has overwhelmed the courts and angered defendants’ lawyers, who say they have no time to meet clients.

The violence erupted after high-school student and union demonstrations. In Paris, the authorised march passed through the capital without major incident. But on the fringes and afterwards, black-clad, masked people rampaged through cities and towns, setting fire to public buildings, bikes and rubbish bins, smashing up restaurants and shops, and looting local and luxury goods stores.

Initial reports blamed the destruction on those protesting against a raft of unaddressed grievances against the president, Emmanuel Macron, and successive governments, including “ultra-left” disrupters spurred on by the France Unbowed leader, Jean-Luc Mélenchon. The reality was, in many cases, more prosaic.

Most of those charged with vandalism, violence, theft, or damaging public or private property appeared to have been what officials have described as “opportunistic delinquents” with mundane rather than political motivations.

The majority were young men. In Paris, 68% of those taken into custody were adults, according to the public prosecutor’s office, not high-school teenagers.

As police escorted the defendants into court from the cells where they had been held since their arrest, it was clear that, apart from black clothing, they could not be categorised. Some were confused, others more confident. Many, like Awa, seemed completely nonplussed at finding themselves before a judge whose first question was: “Do you want to be tried now or later?”

Laure Beccuau, the Paris public prosecutor, told French radio: “The vast majority of those we’ve sent to the courts have never been convicted [before].”
sources.headline: Angry lawyers and bewildered defendants: the fallout from fast-tracking French rioting cases

stories.headline: France reports the first known human case of Shamonda virus, saying there is no wider public-health risk

sources.body: France has reported the first-ever recorded case of a human contracting the Shamonda livestock virus, which is most commonly found in cattle. Public health authorities stressed that there did not appear to be any health risk to the public, adding that the infection had been "an exceptional case" involving a person with a severely compromised immune system.
sources.headline: France reports first human case of Shamonda virus, but says there's no public health risk

sources.body:
Investigations under way to determine whether virus normally found in livestock contributed to man’s death

A man in France has become the first human known to have contracted Shamonda virus, with investigations under way to explore whether it contributed to his death.

Shamonda virus is a type of bunyavirus and is spread by bites from infected midges. According to the Austrian Agency for Health and Food Safety , in animals such as cattle, sheep and goats it can cause diarrhoea, lack of appetite and a decline in milk yield, “as well as abortions and congenital abnormalities in newborn calves, lambs and kids”.

“In Switzerland and Germany, the presence of Shav [Shamonda virus] genetic material has also been reported in the brains of horses that died from neurological symptoms,” the agency said.

The virus has previously been found in farm animals outside Europe, but was first detected in livestock on the continent in the summer. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) said the patient in France was the first recognised human infection.

It also noted that he had already been seriously ill and had a compromised immune system, meaning it was unclear whether the virus played a role in his death this month.

“Investigations into whether the virus caused or contributed to the patient’s death and how the infection was acquired are ongoing,” the ECDC has said.

Prof Tom Solomon, the director of the pandemic institute at the University of Liverpool, said the risk to the general public appeared to be very low. “Shamonda virus has been circulating in animals, particularly cattle, but also sheep, goats, horses and alpacas, for many years, yet this is the first recognised human infection,” he said.

“This suggests that transmission to humans is extremely unusual.”

But unknowns remain, he said: “We don’t know whether healthy people can become infected without developing symptoms, what symptoms the virus might normally cause, or how frequently it might cause serious disease.

“French authorities believe the neurological complications in this patient were very likely linked to the infection, although investigations are continuing. This is clearly concerning, but one exceptional case does not necessarily mean the virus poses a significant threat to the wider population.”

Dr Ben Brennan from the MRC-University of Glasgow’s centre for virus research, said there was currently no evidence of sustained transmission between humans.

“While this discovery warrants further scientific investigation and continued surveillance, it does not currently suggest a significant new public health threat to the UK,” he said. “For most people, there is no reason to change their normal activities or take additional precautions.”
sources.headline: Shamonda virus detected in human for first time in France

Segons les autoritats, s'estan duent a terme investigacions clíniques, biològiques i epidemiològiques amb experts en salut humana, animal i mediambiental.

Els experts que porten el cas creuen que les complicacions cerebrals que se li van manifestar a l'home estan "molt probablement vinculades amb la infecció pel virus de Shamonda".

El Shamonda, que es va identificar per primer cop a Nigèria als anys 60, el transmet un mosquit de tipus Culicoides, principalment al bestiar boví, i es va detectar per primer cop aquest estiu en diferents punts d'Europa, com França.

El cas d'aquest pacient és la primera detecció documentada d'aquest virus en una persona .

La hipòtesi de les autoritats franceses és que hi va haver una contaminació per un mosquit a l'est de França, una zona en què s'havia constatat la circulació de Shamonda a la primavera i estiu.

Ho consideren un "un cas excepcional " en un pacient amb un sistema immunitari molt dèbil. De totes maneres, França ho ha notificat a les instàncies sanitàries internacionals, en concret a l'OMS i al centre Europeu per a la Prevenció i el Control de les Malalties (ECDC).

Segons el Sciencie Media Centre (SMC), la detecció en "un pacient amb un sistema immunitari greument compromès no significa necessàriament que suposi un risc significatiu per a persones que tenen bona salut".

Asseguren que calen "més investigacions per entendre la seva capacitat per infectar persones".
sources.headline: Mor a França una persona infectada pel virus de Shamonda, primer cas detectat en humans

stories.headline: A fake polling firm may have shaped campaign narratives and fundraising in the 2026 elections

sources.body: A new company whose polls had influenced campaign decisions and helped shape the midterms narrative admitted that it was faking its polling data on Tuesday night, setting off a firestorm in the electionsphere. Wedgewood Polls, facing an imminent publication of an investigation from FiftyPlusOne showing it was fabricating its numbers, declared late Tuesday night that it had been an “experimental project” to show how an “entirely fabricated polling firm” could sway public opinion while painting themselves as the good guys. They’d left an impact and been included by multiple credible polling aggregators including The New York Times — and mentioned twice in POLITICO's Morning Score polling roundup. Speculation is flying about what, exactly, Wedgewood was trying to achieve, and there’s still little public information about the defunct company that had crowdfunded thousands of dollars for its fake data. Was it an effort to boost progressives Democrats in primaries? If so, were progressives or Republicans really behind it? Was it being used to game betting markets? Were top operatives using the bogus data to make spending decisions? Were aggregation accounts too quick to jump on posting the data? An email to the account listed on Wedgewood’s X account bounced back, and previous PDFs of polls that were tied to the account are no longer available online. Regardless of what Wedgewood said it was trying to achieve (they remain adamant the project “was never intended to sway an election or permanently mislead the public”) — pollsters, operatives and candidates alike said there were real world implications for posting fake data online. Mallory McMorrow, the unsuccessful Michigan Democratic Senate candidate who dropped out before her primary, said a fake Wedgewood poll that showed her crashing to single-digit support against Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens “dried up” donations, “devastated” volunteers and led to numerous calls to exit the race. “It killed us,” McMorrow wrote on X . “These were some of the absolute worst days on the campaign. Especially for my team. There are no words to explain the morale blow, and nothing I could do or say to my team to fix it.” Jennifer Holdsworth, a Democratic operative who ran a super PAC supporting McMorrow, said the Wedgewood poll “was used by several donors to pull back funding at a time we were being outspent by $80 million.” The account also posted a poll showing democratic socialist Francesca Hong leading in the Wisconsin gubernatorial primary, when there was scant public polling, something that contributed to the narrative she was ahead before the election (which she lost). They also posted a poll showing the Mississippi Senate race within reach, just before Democrats plowed money into the state. Scott Colom, the Democrat running for the seat, blasted the poll to his press list as proof there was “massive momentum” behind him. That led election watchers to argue that Wedgewood’s data was being used to make spending decisions in top outside groups, which elicited a response from Democrats’ main Senate super PAC. “Absolutely not. We don’t make spending or strategic decisions based on external polling,” Lauren French, a spokesperson for Senate Majority PAC, said on X . In its investigation, FiftyPlusOne said it had included Wedgewood in its aggregator because the firm was founded by people who had worked in the polling industry previously. There’s also been broad finger-pointing at the aggregator X accounts that post polls frequently — and sometimes without verifying their accuracy. “You posted our polls multiple times. If you suspected it was fake, why did you post our results?” Wedgewood’s account shot back after Polling USA wrote that “my suspicions about Wedgewood were correct.” The whole ordeal illuminates just how big a problem polling could be in 2028, where both parties will have presidential primaries and polling can shift the narrative on a dime. “What I’m concerned about is essentially information pollution, things that are either intended to skew prediction markets or just straight misinformation flying around,” Charlotte Swasey, a pollster for the Democratic group Searchlight, told POLITICO Magazine recently. “It would be really difficult, especially in a primary, to tell people that what they’re seeing about their preferred candidate isn’t real.” A version of this article first appeared in POLITICO Pro’s Morning Score. sources.headline: How a fake pollster may have moved some 2026 elections

sources.body:
On Tuesday, Oct. 20, FiftyPlusOne reached out to Wedgewood Polls, a self-professed polling firm, with a request for comment on an investigation we had conducted into their alleged survey research. They did not respond to our request, but instead posted a public statement on social media admitting that they had been fabricating data. They also reached out directly in social media DMs minutes before publishing their memo with an official comment: “Fuck you,” plus the name of an individual not affiliated with FiftyPlusOne.

Their statement alleges that FiftyPlusOne, the New York Times , and other poll aggregators did not conduct appropriate vetting of their firm prior to aggregating their polls; this is false. We reached out to them to ask who they were and confirm the methodology statement on their website. We were given two names, Jack Sims and Andrew Prater. We were able to independently confirm that Sims had previous experience in the polling industry and reviewed their methodology statement in detail. It is not atypical for a pollster to leave an existing firm, form their own, and self-fund some surveys to build reputation; we had no reason at the time to believe this case was any different. Wedgewood operated as if it were a legitimate polling firm, including collecting money from donors to conduct crowd-funded polls, and sharing raw survey data (which we now have confirmed was fraudulent) with FiftyPlusOne on Oct. 15, 2026.

Below is the article that we intended to publish tomorrow, Oct. 21, 2026. We had given Wedgewood until midnight to respond to our questions. We have lightly edited the piece to acknowledge Wedgewood Polls’ admission of guilt.

stories.headline: Republicans' large Senate advertising advantage is diluted by their dependence on higher-priced outside-group spending

sources.body: Republicans are banking on a massive cash edge to help save their majority in Congress. But they are losing much of that advantage in an important arena: broadcast TV ads. Republicans have spent $677 million on those ads across 10 key Senate battleground states, compared to $479 million by the Democrats. But the GOP’s money isn’t going nearly as far because they’re more dependent on outside groups that pay much higher rates than candidates. The disparity has helped Democrats stay in the fight for Senate control amid an onslaught of GOP outside spending. In Ohio’s Senate race, Republican groups make up 63% of the $218 million spent. But in spite of their nearly 2-to-1 spending advantage over Democrats, they make up just over half of ads that are on the airwaves, according to data from the tracking service AdImpact. In Texas, Republicans have outspent Democrats by a 3-to-1 margin but have aired just 58% of the ads. And in Michigan, the GOP accounts for 60% of the spending but just over half of the ads. A large part of this discrepancy comes down to the mechanics of broadcast advertising. Candidates, and now political parties thanks to a recent Supreme Court ruling, are entitled to significantly lower rates. That has allowed Democratic candidates — who have posted bonkers fundraising hauls — to offset much of the GOP advantage in super PACs. Republican Senate candidates, on the other hand, struggled overall with their fundraising. And some GOP outside groups bought their ad time later, when it was even more expensive. “There are limitations to the impact of ‘big money’ in politics,” said Sean Cooksey, a Republican and former chair of the Federal Election Commission. “It's a good demonstration of the economics of campaign fundraising. Hard dollars really just go so much further.” The disparity also shows “the Republican overreliance on outside groups,” said Ian Russell, a Democratic admaker. “You get an eye-popping dollar amount, but it doesn't actually translate into as many spots as you would think relative to a well-financed candidate,” Russell said. “[Republicans] were just hoping that they could spend their way out of everything that was going wrong for them. But the problem is, their issues run much deeper than a few ad buys can fix. Especially when you've got monster fundraising hauls from the Democratic side.” Republicans in House and Senate races have long been more dependent on outside groups and megadonors, and for multiple cycles have seen their cash advantage undercut by fundraising strength from individual Democratic candidates. But that trend is particularly pronounced this year given the combination of Republican super PAC money and their candidates’ struggles. In 2024, Republican outside groups spent only about 15% more than Democrats on TV ads across House and Senate general election contests, according to a POLITICO analysis of AdImpact data. This cycle, GOP outside groups have spent 7% more. In a few states, the discrepancy between dollars and airtime is less stark. Republicans account for 60% of the spending in Maine’s Senate race and an equal percentage of the ads, according to AdImpact. That’s in part because Sen. Susan Collins has outraised her Democratic opponent Troy Jackson over the whole cycle, although Jackson, who didn’t launch his campaign until July, raised far more in the third quarter. The numbers show the shifting dynamics of campaign strategy after the Supreme Court opened the floodgates to more spending from parties by granting them the lower advertising rate. Republicans have been faster to take advantage of the new rules: Major coordinated spending efforts from the NRSC and RNC have helped their side significantly this cycle. Republicans have far outspent Democrats on Senate party-coordinated Senate advertising, $90 million to $34.6 million across TV, radio and digital ads, according to data from AdImpact. “If I were the leader of either party, I would say you shouldn't give a dollar, you shouldn't give a single penny to these super PACs until you've maxed out to the party committee,” Cooksey said. Some Republicans say that strategic errors have contributed to erasing their cash edge. A number of GOP strategists have also privately griped that MAGA Inc. — one of the major outside groups backing their candidates — bought TV airtime too late, forcing them to pay even higher rates and further draining resources and increasing the price of reaching voters. Republicans fretted for months about whether Trump’s well-financed super PAC, MAGA Inc., would get involved . The group has since spent heavily but only launched its first general election ad buys in September. “There is no question MAGA Inc. should have bought ads earlier in the cycle,” said one national GOP operative who was granted anonymity to discuss party strategy, noting that rates across the country increase as Election Day nears. Other top GOP outside groups, like the Senate Leadership Fund and the Congressional Leadership Fund, made their early advertising reservations much earlier in the cycle than MAGA Inc. Trump allies waved away that criticism. A person familiar with the Trump operation’s midterm planning, granted anonymity to discuss strategy, said it’s "indisputable that the spending from the Trump political effort has kept us competitive in many Senate races.” MAGA Inc. declined to comment. Still, GOP outside groups are utilizing their cash advantage in some underappreciated ways. Republican super PACs have massively outspent their Democratic counterparts on mail — roughly $157 million to $35 million for the general election — according to a POLITICO analysis of independent expenditure filings submitted to the Federal Election Commission. That’s led by a whopping $44 million in spending on mail across 24 races from the Trump-aligned No Going Back PAC, along with $23.8 million across 20 races from Elon Musk’s America PAC. GOP-aligned super PACs have also spent more than Democratic ones on phone calls and text messages, the data shows.
sources.headline: Why Republicans’ massive cash advantage is evaporating on the airwaves

stories.headline: Georgia Republicans look to self-funding gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson to limit wider midterm losses

sources.body: Georgia Republicans are counting on Rick Jackson to save them from a wipeout in November — if President Donald Trump doesn’t get in the way. The billionaire health care executive and political newcomer has spent nearly $200 million since he entered the Georgia governor’s race earlier this year. That’s boosted GOP hopes as many in the party have all but given up on the state’s marquee Senate race, where Rep. Mike Collins is struggling to close the gap against a formidably well-funded Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff. Republicans worry that their open contests for attorney general and lieutenant governor as well as control of the state general assembly could be in peril in a larger blue wave. But Jackson’s deep pockets are being tested against a difficult political environment for Republicans, weighed down by unpopular Trump actions, including the war in Iran. And some in the GOP worry that the president’s repeated visits to Georgia could only make the situation worse. “I don't know that Trump coming helps Republicans more so than it excites Democrats, especially in a wave election year, and so becomes and becomes a catch-22 for Republican candidates,” said Jason Shepherd, a former Cobb County chair who is supporting Jackson. One Georgia-based Republican strategist who is not involved in the gubernatorial race posited that Trump’s dual appearances in the state almost certainly did more harm than help. They, like others in this article, were granted anonymity to speak openly about the race to avoid reprisals. “Every piece of data that I've seen, it is not MAGA Republicans that are unmotivated to vote in this election,” the person said. “All the data that I've seen is that the undecideds in our marquee races, and specifically in the governor's race, have a very, very negative opinion of the president. So, I can't really rationalize a case for how it would be helpful.” Jackson, for his part, has carefully navigated his relationship with the president and has not publicly broken with him on policy like other battleground Republicans. But he has not mentioned the president in any of the nearly 150 ads he’s run in the general election, according to an analysis of data from tracking firm AdImpact. Shortly after the RNC announced that Trump would return to the state this weekend, Jackson’s team said in a statement that the candidate will be campaigning in a different part of Georgia. And during his only televised gubernatorial debate on Oct. 6 against Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, Jackson never name-dropped the president — despite his opponent invoking Trump’s name eight times. Instead, the Republican mentioned popular outgoing GOP Gov. Brian Kemp five times and focused on Bottoms’ tenure as mayor of Atlanta during the Covid-19 pandemic. “It’s been proven time and again that when the message is on Georgia, and the results under Brian Kemp and the conservative vision and road map that's been laid out here, that we win in Georgia. When the focus is on D.C. and personal politics, we lose,” said Cole Muzio, president of the conservative Frontline Policy Action group .  The Jackson campaign declined to comment for this story. “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party,” White House spokesperson Davis Ingle said in a statement. Natalie Baldassarre, a spokesperson for the Republican National Committee, said in a statement that Republicans “are laser focused on winning, and our candidates will run the races necessary to best represent their districts and prevent Democrats from taking control." Jackson is one of several Republicans across the country who now must balance between keeping the president close enough to turn out Republican base voters, but not so closely as to alienate the center. Though many Georgia Republicans see Jackson as their de-facto ticket-topper, they don’t see his win as a guarantee against Bottoms, the former Atlanta mayor, in a finicky battleground state like Georgia. Jackson has outspent Bottoms nearly 5-to-1 in the final stretch of the race but still remains in a close race in public polling . And yet, without him, Republicans fear the bottom would have already fallen out on races up and down the ballot, given how poorly Collins is performing in polls against Ossoff. Republicans’ top Senate super PAC, Senate Leadership Fund, was dark in Georgia last week , a sign the race may be slipping out of reach. “If Rick Jackson weren't running, we would all be in a lot of trouble,” said Stephen Lawson, a Georgia-based Republican strategist and Jackson ally. “He’s our best hope at keeping the state red.” A second Georgia-based Republican strategist, who is working on other races in the state, underscored how Jackson’s money is keeping the party afloat. “There is no question in my mind that without the extra $150 million he spent in his general election, that the ticket would be lost,” this person said. “That is the only reason there's still a fight to be had.” But, this person cautioned, the race is still very much a toss-up, and Jackson’s victory will rely on a large share of Georgia voters choosing to split their ballots between Ossoff for Senate and Jackson for governor. Jackson’s allies are optimistic that a significant number of voters will do just that. A private statewide poll reviewed by POLITICO found that roughly 19% of Georgia voters say they are definitely or likely to cast a vote for at least one Democrat and one Republican — a potentially significant pool of crossover voters that could power two very different results in the marquee contests. Whether the sheer force of Jackson’s spending will prove successful enough to overcome Trump is a microcosm of the larger issue his party is experiencing across the country: National Republicans, flush with cash, hold an enormous financial advantage over Democrats. But money alone may not be enough to insulate candidates in battlegrounds or even in traditionally red territory. “I don't know that Republicans across the country should feel as bullish about the cash influx that we've gotten because it didn't work here,” said the first GOP operative. “In terms of actively moving races in our favor, it at least didn't work here.” In the last month, as Bottoms began to spend more heavily on the air amid Jackson's spending advantage, her campaign has noted that polling has started to move marginally in her favor — even if the race remains largely within the margin of error . Her high name ID, as well as cash spent after the primary to define her early, are helping. “Rick Jackson has spent $200 million in this campaign but all the money in the world can’t hide the fact that he would be a lackey for Donald Trump,” TaNisha Cameron, a spokesperson for Bottoms, said in a statement. “Despite being outspent, Keisha’s message is breaking through and she has the momentum in this race right when it matters." Jackson is making more of an effort to tie himself closely to Kemp, who won over moderates and independents in his 2022 reelection for governor and has an approval rating that sits 30 points higher than the president’s in Georgia, according to a recent poll by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution . Kemp, for his part, has continued to be a presence on the trail for Jackson, including joining him on a statewide tour earlier this month and appearing in at least three TV ads for the campaign. But Jackson’s pathway to victory requires him to not only secure crossover voters that may support Ossoff in the Senate race or the type of voters who broke for Kemp, but also turn out the MAGA base who powered the president’s two presidential victories in the perennial battleground. The president is intent on still showing up for him. Shortly after Jackson dispatched Trump’s initially preferred candidate, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, in June’s primary runoff, the president was quick to praise Jackson as standing “strong with ‘TRUMP.’” And in subsequent posts on Truth Social, Trump has called the health care executive a “good friend.” Trump, onstage Friday, called Jackson a “great businessman,” before adding: “I’ve been watching you, you are good, and he never did this before. He did it because he wants to straighten out things and he’s an amazing, an amazing story.” Aaron Pellish contributed to this report.
sources.headline: Rick Jackson is the GOP’s best hope in Georgia right now

stories.headline: Spain's PP uses AI-generated videos impersonating socialist figures in an escalating election campaign tactic

sources.body: <p>No solo hay 10 horas de diferencia entre los dos vídeos. El primero, del PSOE, se publicó en la cuenta oficial de Pedro Sánchez a las 8.29 de la mañana de este miércoles, <a href="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-21/milei-saca-el-programa-de-la-motosierra-en-el-casino-ante-jaime-de-marichalar-ramon-tamames-y-figuras-del-pp-y-vox.html" target="_self" rel="" title="https://elpais.com/espana/elecciones-generales/2026-10-21/milei-saca-el-programa-de-la-motosierra-en-el-casino-ante-jaime-de-marichalar-ramon-tamames-y-figuras-del-pp-y-vox.html">justo antes de la ponencia de Javier Milei en el Casino de Madrid</a>. Y el segundo, del PP, pasadas las diez de la noche. Pero uno es real: grabado con cámaras, micrófonos y editado por un equipo de comunicadores audiovisuales. Y el otro, no: está generado por una aplicación de inteligencia artificial. Es más, es la primera vez que un partido político en España usa esta estrategia para suplantar la identidad y la voz de dirigentes y figuras políticas, como José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero, Begoña Gómez, la exportavoz socialista Montse Mínguez y hasta José Luis Ábalos, entre otros. En el caso de este último, quizá sea el más realista y parece que habla él mismo de verdad. sources.headline: El PP da un paso más en su campaña y suplanta la identidad de Begoña Gómez, Zapatero y Ábalos: “¿Irse de putas? Sí, soy zurdo”

sources.body:
“Sí, soy zurdo. Y a mucha honra”, advertía ayer Pedro Sánchez en un vídeo de precampaña que protagonizó con motivo de la polémica visita a España del presidente de Argentina, Javier Milei , en la que dedicó graves insultos al presidente del Gobierno como “impresentable dictador”, “liberticida” y “delincuente ladrón” entre otros improperios.

Si el jefe del Ejecutivo quiso exprimir con ese vídeo la visita del mandatario argentino, que podía incomodar al PP, los populares han contraatacado este jueves con otra campaña con un formato muy parecido pero hecho con inteligencia artificial (IA) y usando la imagen y la voz de líderes socialistas o del entorno del Gobierno admitiendo, en algunos casos, delitos, por los que han sido juzgados, se les juzgará o por los que se les investiga. El PP abre así un camino inédito que levanta no pocas dudas sobre su legitimidad e incluso legalidad.

La primera en aparecer en el vídeo, encabezado con el lema “Lerdos y orgullosos” en contraposición al hashtag #zurdosyorgullosos usado ayer, es Begoña Gómez, a quien se le hace decir: “Si tener una cátedra gracias a que mi marido es el presidente es de zurdos, pues sí, soy zurda”. La esposa de Pedro Sánchez está a la espera de juicio después de una controvertida instrucción del juez Juan Carlos Peinado.

“Si irse de p***s y cobrar comisiones ilegales es de zurdos, pues sí, soy zurdo”, dice un simulado exministro de Transportes José Luis Ábalos, condenado a 24 años de cárcel por el caso mascarillas.

El expresidente José Luis Rodríguez Zapatero aparece diciendo “si esconder joyas en una caja fuerte es de zurdos… pues sí, soy zurdo”. Esa circunstancia forma parte de la investigación que lleva a cabo el juez Calama sobre el rescate de la aerolínea Plus Ultra.

“Si contratar a unos matones para quitar de en medio a una jueza es de zurdos, pues sí, soy zurda”, señala una simulada Leire Díez, conocida como la fontanera del PSOE e investigada por el juez Santiago Pedraz por presuntos intentos de hacer descarrilar investigaciones al entorno del PSOE como la del hermano del presidente.

A la exportavoz del PSOE Montse Mínguez, el PP le hace decir “si usar la vivienda como arma política mientras oculto que mi novio tiene más de 30 pisos es de zurdos, pues sí, soy zurda”, aludiendo al motivo de su reciente dimisión. Y el último en aparecer es un simulado Santos Cerdán, ex secretario general del PSOE diciendo “si cobrar mordidas y pertenecer a una banda criminal es de zurdos, pues sí, soy zurdo”.

La portavoz del PSOE, Rebeca Torró, ha calificado el vídeo del PP en decalaraciones a La SER de “lamentable” y ha acusado a los populares de mantener una estrategia basada en la descalificación personal. “Llevan cuatro años de insultos y mentiras y ahora utilizan otro instrumento, que es la IA, porque no tienen otra cosa que el insulto permanente”, ha asegurado.

El formato replica el vídeo distribuido ayer por los socialistas en el que Sánchez decía que “hay quienes creen que nos insultan llamándonos “zurdos” o “zurdas”, aludiendo a la forma pretendidamente despectiva que Milei usa para referirse a los socialistas. Acto seguido el presidente señalaba las iniciativas que ha tomado su Gobierno en benefocio de la sociedad para poner en valor el hecho de ser zurdo, es decir socialista, lo que supone un motivo de orgullo y honra.
sources.headline: El PP crea con IA vídeos falsos de socialistas admitiendo delitos

sources.body: <p>No es la primera vez que sucede. El portavoz nacional del PP, Borja Sémper

La dirección nacional del PP no quiere caer en el marco del PSOE de situar la visita de Javier Milei en el centro de la precampaña. Borja Sémper, portavoz de los populares, ha acusado al PSOE de usar el paso por Madrid del presidente argentino para desviar el foco de los “problemas de los ciudadanos”. “No hablamos de las lonas que pone un partido político”, ha señalado Sémper, haciendo referencia a que los socialistas desplegaron una lona gigante en la sede de la calle Ferraz y usaron camisetas en el acto en Burgos de Pedro Sánchez bajo el lema de “orgullosos de ser zurdos” en respuesta a la visita de Milei.

El presidente argentino siempre usa el concepto “zurdo” para dirigirse a la izquierda y criticarla. Y, ayer en su visita a Madrid, fue  contundente en su rechazo a Sánchez, al llamarle "dictador" . No obstante, en el PP se mantienen una postura propia ya que entienden que el PSOE trata de usar electoralmente el conflicto con Milei. En este punto, cabe recordar que es la postura que ya tuvo el PP cuando Óscar Puente dio inicio al cruce de descalificaciones con Milei en mayo de 2024: el ministro acusó al presidente argentino de “ingestas de sustancias” y la escalada verbal acabó en una crisis diplomática.

En este sentido, el propio Sémper ha hecho referencia al Gobierno y Puente por sus formas. “¿Estamos en España para dar lecciones cuando hay ministros que llaman ratas a periodistas? ¿Estamos en España de verdad para señalar a alguien desde fuera? ¿No tenemos que mirarnos primero a nosotros?”, ha planteado.

En todo caso, Sémper ha fijado la postura del partido y ha asegurado que, desde el “máximo respeto” a Milei, el PP solo se centra en lo que “ha hecho” Sánchez en los últimos ocho años y en hablar de Alberto Núñez Feijóo y del “futuro de España”. “Yo entiendo que la política es un show y es un espectáculo, lamentablemente. Y yo entiendo que hay una intencionalidad de que no hablemos de los problemas de los españoles. Pero yo voy a hablar de los problemas de los españoles”, ha afirmado.

“No voy a hablar de quién viene y quién deja de venir a España”, ha añadido, y ha señalado que su intención es hablar de problemas como que “mucha gente tiene miedo para llegar al fin de mes” o “tiene problemas para encontrar una vivienda a un precio razonable”. “Mucha gente que nos está viendo ahora tiene problemas serios y profundos como para que yo me dedique a jugar a esta teatralización en la que se ha convertido la política”, ha añadido. ”Me niego a pasar por la vergüenza de hablar de algo que mucha gente que nos está viendo no se siente interpelada”, ha zanjado.

Dentro del PP, en todo caso, hay diferentes posturas sobre Milei. El propio Xavier García Albiol, alcalde de Badalona y candidato por Barcelona al Congreso, se ha pronunciado y ha criticado las formas del presidente argentino. “Seguramente no tiene las formas más adecuadas para ser el presidente de un país. Hablo de las formas. Después, sobre el contenido, cada uno en su país sabe cómo va. Al final, si Milei ha ganado las elecciones en Argentina, tenemos que respetar las decisiones”, ha dicho en declaraciones a la Ser .

stories.headline: Police find 74 migrants, including 10 children, crowded into a Ceuta apartment

sources.body:
Una operación de la Policía Nacional desarrollada el pasado martes ha permitido localizar a 74 migrantes en situación irregular hacinados y con lesiones de mordeduras de perros en un piso en el barrio del Príncipe de Ceuta, entre ellos diez menores, en una investigación que ha dejado un detenido que pretendía trasladar a estas personas a la península.

Según ha informado la Policía Nacional, la operación requirió un importante despliegue policial debido a la complejidad del lugar donde se encuentra el inmueble y se ha saldado con la detención de un ciudadano ceutí considerado el principal responsable de una organización criminal dedicada, presuntamente, al favorecimiento de la inmigración y otras actividades delictivas.

Durante el operativo los agentes han localizado a 54 hombres, 10 mujeres y 10 menores de edad no acompañados, lo que suma un total de 74 personas alojadas en el inmueble investigado. Al detenido se le imputan delitos de favorecimiento de la inmigración irregular, contra los derechos de los trabajadores, lesiones a menor y explotación laboral de menores.

Las pesquisas policiales han permitido obtener indicios de que algunos menores alojados en el inmueble podrían haber sido víctimas de agresiones físicas, incluyendo lesiones ocasionadas por mordeduras de un perro .

Asimismo, los agentes investigan la posible explotación laboral, tanto de menores como mayores de edad, que habrían sido utilizados para realizar diferentes tareas y trabajos, aprovechándose de su situación de necesidad y vulnerabilidad. "A las dificultades derivadas de la ubicación del inmueble se ha sumado la peligrosidad atribuida a la organización criminal, cuyos integrantes cuentan con numerosos antecedentes policiales", ha señalado la Policía en una nota de prensa.

El elevado número de personas localizadas durante la intervención se enmarca en un contexto de intensificación de la presión policial, que ha acabado con el desalojo de los asentamientos en la playa Benítez y El Trampolín, según la Policía. El desmantelamiento de los asentamientos ha propiciado el desplazamiento de una parte de los migrantes que permanecían en ellos hacia otros puntos de la ciudad, entre ellos el barrio de El Príncipe.

Ante esta situación, la Policía Nacional ha señalado que mantiene una "intensa actividad operativa", tanto en las inmediaciones como en la misma barriada. La operación ha supuesto, además, un importante golpe a la infraestructura logística del entramado criminal, que mantenía alojadas a numerosas personas en el inmueble a la espera de una oportunidad para facilitar su traslado irregular a la península.

La investigación se ha desarrollado gracias a la coordinación de las diferentes plantillas policiales repartidas tanto por la costa andaluza como a nivel central que están trabajando conjuntamente con la Fiscalía contra la lucha del tráfico ilícito de migrantes. Este jueves, el detenido ha sido puesto a disposición de la autoridad judicial.

sources.headline: Álvarez de Toledo y Sémper serán los números dos y tres de Feijóo en la lista por Madrid

sources.body:
La diputada del PP Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo y el portavoz de la formación Borja Sémper acompañarán al líder, Alberto Núñez Feijóo , en los puestos 2 y 3 de la lista de Madrid . Los dos representan "formas distintas de entender España y ambos han atravesado por diferentes etapas en el PP", señalan los 'populares' en un comunicado en el que han dado a conocer la decisión este jueves cuando quedan cuatro días para que acabe el plazo para presentar las listas a las elecciones del 29 de noviembre.

En el PP están "muy orgullosos" de que los dos sientan el PP como "su casa" y además "decidan dar la cara por sus ideas " encabezando junto a Feijóo la lista de Madrid, en un "proyecto amplio" en el que "caben todas las sensibilidades", una "formación abierta donde los matices y los acentos no incomodan a nadie, sino que enriquecen a todos", señala el comunicado.

“ 🔴ÚLTIMA HORA | Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo y Borja Sémper irán en las listas del PP como número dos y tres por Madrid ▪️El anuncio ha llegado con un vídeo del partido en el que destaca que forman el "mejor equipo por Madrid" 🎙️@dafevila 🖊️https://t.co/BEA4bV6IWZ https://t.co/FBj26mVW8B “

La incógnita de quiénes iban a encabezar las papeletas se ha mantenido hasta este jueves, a sólo unos días de que acabe el plazo para presentar las listas, que la Junta Electoral Central (JEC) hará oficiales el 2 de noviembre.

Y aunque desde Génova han guardado silencio, el nombre de Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo, hasta ahora portavoz adjunta del PP en el Congreso, y una de las voces más beligerantes contra el Gobierno de Pedro Sánchez era uno de los que más sonaban.

La diputada ha expresado su agradecimiento a Feijóo "por el liderazgo y la confianza " al nombrarla número dos de la lista por Madrid a través de un mensaje publicado en la red social X, y ha defendido "un Gobierno decente, inteligente y valiente" para España. "Y lo tendrá", agrega.

“ Gracias, @NunezFeijoo Por el liderazgo y la confianza. España necesita un Gobierno decente, inteligente y valiente. Y lo tendrá. “

El portavoz nacional del PP, Borja Sémper , ha reaccionado tras hacerse oficial su nombramiento asegurando que es "un honor" contar con la confianza de Feijóo y "sobre todo una inmensa responsabilidad" poder compartir con él cartel en la lista de Madrid.

“ Contar con la confianza de @NunezFeijoo es un honor y, sobre todo, una inmensa responsabilidad. Haremos una España mejor y repararemos el daño causado. Unidad, esperanza e ilusión. “

En una entrevista en Telecinco, el también vicesecretario de Cultura y Deporte del PP ha dicho que con Álvarez de Toledo comparte "lo esencial" y que más allá de nombres, lo más importante es ofrecer a los españoles "un Gobierno de reformas y no de escándalos".

Así se ha pronunciado en una entrevista en el programa de Ana Rosa en Telecinco. Ante la apreciación de que son dos sensibilidades muy distintas la suya y la de Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo, ha señalado que el PP es un partido que representa una "amplia mayoría social " y no son un "partido de nicho", sino uno que "quiere parecerse a España".

sources.body:
El presidente del Partido Popular, Alberto Núñez Feijóo, junto a la portavoz adjunta en la cámara, Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo.

Alberto Núñez Feijóo llevará como dos a Cayetana Álvarez de Toledo y como tres a Borja Sémper en la lista electoral por la Comunidad de Madrid. De esta manera, el PP incluye dos perfiles distintos en la circunscripción de la capital española, donde se escogen a 38 diputados de los 350 que forman el Congreso.

De hecho, fuentes del PP reivindican que es el partido de Feijóo “es un proyecto amplio en el que caben todas las sensibilidades”. “Somos una formación abierta donde los matices y los acentos no incomodan a nadie, sino que enriquecen a todos”, añaden, antes de asegurar que Álvarez de Toledo y Sémper “representan formas distintas de entender España y ambos han atravesado por diferentes etapas en el PP”.

En este sentido, con Álvarez de Toledo, los populares aspiran a atraer votante más descontento que esté en la frontera entre el PP y Vox, mientras que con Sémper, pueden dirigirse sobre todo a los electores de centro que hayan elegido en el pasado a Pedro Sánchez y ahora quieran cambiar. De hecho, en privado, en el PP, señalan que están volcados en ir a la búsqueda del voto de centro porque es el que permite que haya transvase del bloque de la izquierda al de la derecha y puede voltear el resultado de las elecciones de 2023, donde la derecha se quedó a cuatro escaños de formar Gobierno.

”Las diferencias en el PP no se combaten, se respetan. Y Feijóo es un candidato en el que pueden confluir españoles de diferente signo y condición. Como siempre dijimos, la España sin muros”, exponen los populares. “Estamos muy orgullosos de que las personas que acompañan al presidente representen perfiles distintos de ciudadanos diversos. Y, sin embargo, unidos ante el reto de hacer de nuestro país un lugar mejor”, añaden.

Hasta el último momento ha habido dudas sobre quién sería el número dos de Feijóo por Madrid, aunque en los últimos días todo ya apuntaba a Álvarez de Toledo. De hecho, ya ayer, OkDiario adelantó el nombre. La alternativa a Álvarez de Toledo que más sonaba es Alma Ezcurra, un perfil muy parecido y con mucho peso en el PP: de hecho, es quien está liderando la elaboración del programa electoral, aunque ahora es eurodiputada.

Álvarez de Toledo, nacida en Madrid en 1974, es historiadora, licenciada y doctorada en la Universidad de Oxford y entró en política hace justo 20 años de la mano de Ángel Acebes, quien era secretario general del PP de Mariano Rajoy. No obstante, cuando adquirió más peso en política fue en la época de Pablo Casado, cuando llegó a ser portavoz del partido en el Congreso. No obstante, fue destituida del cargo al cabo de un año.

En la anterior legislatura -2019-2023-, fue número uno por Barcelona, mientras que en la que ha terminado ahora fue por Madrid como número seis.

Sémper, por su parte, volvió a la política tras su paso por la empresa privada por Feijóo y ahora ejerce de portavoz del partido. Nacido en Gipuzkoa en 1976, había hecho toda su trayectoria política en el PP vasco hasta que dio el salto en 2023 a Madrid y en las pasadas elecciones ya acudió como tres por Madrid. Sémper dejó la política en 2020 para irse a de director de Relaciones por la consultora EY.
